---
title: "Data protection and security"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

SRTR standard analysis files (SAFs) are restricted data. This page says what
sRtr does to help keep them protected, what it does not do, and what is
planned. It is a first version: sRtr's protections are still being built, and
each one is added here when it arrives. Planned items link to their GitHub
issue, where the design is discussed; the
[data protection project](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/303)
gathers them.

Nothing here replaces your data use agreement (DUA) or your data security
plan. They decide what you may do; sRtr can only make the safe path easier.

# At a glance

```{r protections, echo = FALSE}
repo <- "https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr"
sections <- c(
  "reads-and-writes" = "Where sRtr reads and writes",
  "version-control" = "Keep SAFs out of version control",
  "sharing-results" = "Share results, not records",
  "contributing" = "Contributing without SRTR data"
)
statuses <- c("in place", "planned")

# The table is hand-edited, so check it before drawing anything from it. Any
# problem stops the site build with a message naming the row.
protections <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/protections.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = "character"
)
problems <- character()
absent <- setdiff(c("section", "protection", "status", "issue"), names(protections))
if (length(absent) > 0) {
  problems <- paste0("protections.csv: missing column ", absent)
} else {
  row <- seq_len(nrow(protections))
  bad <- function(test, what) {
    if (any(test)) sprintf("protections.csv: %s in row %s", what, row[test]) else character()
  }
  issue <- trimws(protections$issue)
  problems <- c(
    bad(!protections$section %in% names(sections), "unknown section"),
    bad(!nzchar(trimws(protections$protection)), "blank protection"),
    bad(!protections$status %in% statuses, "status must be \"in place\" or \"planned\""),
    bad(nzchar(issue) & !grepl("^[0-9]+$", issue), "issue is not a number"),
    bad(protections$status == "planned" & !nzchar(issue), "planned protection without an issue")
  )
}
if (length(problems) > 0) stop(paste(problems, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)

protections$section <- factor(protections$section, levels = names(sections))
protections <- protections[order(protections$section), ]
shown <- data.frame(
  Topic = sprintf("[%s](#%s)", sections[as.character(protections$section)], protections$section),
  Protection = protections$protection,
  Status = ifelse(
    nzchar(trimws(protections$issue)),
    sprintf("%s ([#%s](%s/issues/%s))", protections$status,
            protections$issue, repo, protections$issue),
    protections$status
  )
)
# Name each topic once, on its first row.
shown$Topic[duplicated(protections$section)] <- ""
knitr::kable(shown, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Your agreement sets the rules {#your-agreement}

SRTR releases SAFs only under a signed DUA, and every request that needs a DUA
must also have a data security plan and a research plan ([SRTR
2026](#ref-srtr-requests)). Those documents decide where the files may be
stored, who may see them, and what may be reported from them. sRtr cannot
check any of this.

SRTR's public pages state no rule on the smallest count you may report. The
signed DUA is not public, so read yours for a reporting clause. For data
linked to Medicare records, the CMS cell size suppression policy applies: no
count from 1 to 10, and no number from which such a count can be worked out
([CMS 2020](#ref-cms)). For SRTR data alone, masking counts below 11 is
common practice rather than a published SRTR rule. sRtr's articles follow it.

Nothing on this page is legal advice. A protection marked "in place" lowers
a risk; it does not show that an analysis meets your agreement.

# Where sRtr reads and writes {#reads-and-writes}

- **Reading.** `load_srtr_file()` reads SAFs only from the folder you set
  with `set_srtr_wd()` (the `SRTR_WD` environment variable), on your own
  computer.
- **The network.** sRtr sends nothing from your files anywhere. Only two
  functions use the network, and both download public map layers from HRSA
  without sending anything about your data:
  `get_hrsa_transplant_centers()` and `get_hrsa_opo_service_areas()`. The
  [Coverage gain](geographic-coverage-gain.html) article also downloads
  public Census data, with your own API key.
- **Writing.** sRtr's functions write nothing outside R's temporary folder
  (`tempdir()`) unless you give them a path. One function writes outside it
  when you ask: `set_srtr_wd(path, permanent = TRUE)` saves the folder's
  path, not any data, to your `~/.Renviron` file.

Keep the SAF folder where your security plan says. In particular, keep it out
of any folder tracked by git, and out of folders that a cloud service
synchronizes, unless your plan covers that service.

**Planned:** `set_srtr_wd()` will warn when the folder is inside a git
repository and not ignored
([#294](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/294)).

# Keep SAFs out of version control {#version-control}

A SAF, or any file made from one, that is committed to git is copied to
every clone and stays in the history after it is deleted. Pushing it to a
private repository is still a disclosure.

sRtr's own repository has two guards. Its `.gitignore` file keeps SAF
formats out of commits, and a check on GitHub fails on SAF formats, on
text files whose headers have SRTR identifier columns, and on files over 5 MB.
You can add the same patterns to the `.gitignore` of your own analysis
project:

```
# SRTR data: never commit
*.[sS][aA][sS]7[bB][dD][aA][tT]
*.[sS][aA][sS]7[bB][cC][aA][tT]
*.[xX][pP][tT]
*.[pP][aA][rR][qQ][uU][eE][tT]
*.[fF][eE][aA][tT][hH][eE][rR]
*.[aA][rR][rR][oO][wW]
*.[dD][tT][aA]
*.[sS][aA][vV]
```

These patterns catch the usual file formats only. They do not catch
`.rds`, `.RData` or `.csv` files you write from a SAF, and `git add -f`
overrides them. Keep files made from SAFs in the same protected folder as
the SAFs, not in the project.

**Planned** ([#294](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/294);
function names are provisional):

- a function that scans a project folder for files that look like SRTR
  data;
- a check when sRtr is attached, which warns, naming paths only, about such
  files that git does not ignore (on by default, with an option to turn it
  off);
- helpers that add the patterns above to your project's `.gitignore` and
  install a commit hook that runs the scan on staged files.

# Share results, not records {#sharing-results}

Share aggregate results only, never rows. Mask any count from 1 to 10, and do
not share a total beside masked parts, or two counts that differ by a little,
because a reader can work out the small count by subtraction. [Checking
sRtr on your own SAFs](checking-your-safs.html#share-counts-only) explains
each rule with code.

**Planned:** a function that checks tables, model output and figures for
small cells, with the threshold set by an option
([#295](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/295)), and small-cell
flags in sRtr's summary functions
([#11](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/11)).

# AI assistants and help requests {#assistants}

A chat with an AI assistant, a GitHub issue, a forum post and an email to a
colleague outside your agreement are all disclosures. When you ask for help:

- share your code, column names and masked counts;
- do not paste rows, printed data frames, or the output of `head()`,
  `str()` or `View()` on SAF data, and do not attach files made from SAFs;
- treat sRtr's error and warning messages, and test failures, as output from
  your files: they can include exact counts, and some quote values from a
  column (for example, codes that no format lists). Before you share one,
  replace every count, value and identifier it contains, or reproduce the
  message on a few made-up rows and share that instead.

An assistant that can read your files or run commands on your computer can
read the SAF folder too. Do not give it access to that folder unless your
security plan covers the tool.

# Contributing without SRTR data {#contributing}

sRtr is developed without SRTR data. Its tests run on small, made-up data;
the tests that need real SAFs skip unless `SRTR_LIVE_TESTS` and `SRTR_WD`
are set, and are run only by people whose own DUA covers the files, on
their own computers. Results from those runs are shared as masked aggregate
counts. [Development and how to contribute](development.html) lists work
that needs no SAFs.

**Planned:** a contributor guide to keeping SRTR data out of the repository
([#94](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/94)), a synthetic SAF
generator for tests and examples
([#1](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/1)), and public
center-level tables for examples that need no DUA
([#13](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues/13)).

# What sRtr does not do {#limits}

- sRtr is not a secure computing environment. It does not encrypt files,
  control who can open them or keep an audit log; your institution's
  environment provides those.
- Its checks, now and planned, look for common patterns. A clean check does
  not show that a folder or a repository holds no patient data.
- It does not decide what your DUA allows.
